Born rule probabilities can be given a coherent role in an Everettian interpretation, but that role cannot simply be the chance that one branch alone will be created. In the many-worlds interpretation, unitary measurement produces all of the decohering outcome components. The question is why their squared amplitudes should govern rational expectation, typical recorded frequencies or concern for future observers.
For a state ∑i​ci​∣si​⟩ and a measuring apparatus, the resulting correlated state has components ci​∣si​⟩∣Ai​⟩. The squared norms wi​=∣ci​∣2 supply additive branch weights. They are preserved by unitary refinements of an outcome into orthogonal subcomponents: if a branch splits internally, its descendants' weights sum to its original weight. Everett's original paper introduces the relative-state description and a measure associated with the statistical analysis; this should not be confused with an independent stochastic collapse law.[ref]
A simple example shows why counting branches is not an alternative rule without further structure. Begin with
∣ψ⟩=3​1​∣A⟩+32​​∣B⟩.
(167)
If an irrelevant environment interaction refines B into two orthogonal components of equal amplitude, there are now three displayed components, each of amplitude 1/3​. The total weight of B is still 2/3. Counting displayed components instead changes A's assigned share from 1/2 to 1/3, merely because the description has resolved additional environmental detail. Real decoherent branching is approximate and has no unique fundamental branch count. Squared norm, in contrast, respects such refinements.
There are at least two ways to understand the remaining epistemic issue. An observer may have self-locating uncertainty in Everettian quantum mechanics, especially after branching but before accessing a record: the uncertainty concerns which centred observer situation is theirs, not ignorance of the global wave function. Alternatively, a decision-theoretic account can ask how a present observer should value all future successors without assuming that exactly one successor is uniquely them. These are distinct proposals, and the second does not become incoherent simply because the first is disputed.
David Wallace's decision-theoretic programme argues that suitable rationality and measurement-equivalence assumptions lead to expected-utility weights equal to squared amplitudes. The assumptions, including the appropriate neutrality of the measurement implementation, do real work.[ref] A critic can question whether the constraints already privilege the desired measure or whether a preference theorem establishes the empirical role of chance. The defender must answer those objections; unitarity and normalization alone do not automatically turn a deterministic global theory into ordinary single-outcome randomness.
Repeated experiments add a consistency check. With Born weights, the total weight of frequency records is binomial and concentrates near the Born frequency as the number of trials increases. Yet calling the high-weight records typical already uses a measure, so this is not by itself a noncircular derivation of the weighting rule. The balanced conclusion is that Born probabilities are not meaningless in Everettian quantum mechanics: they can organize credence, decisions and typical records. Their status requires an argued connection between branch weights and those roles, rather than a bare appeal either to all outcomes happening or to the algebraic identity ∑i​∣ci​∣2=1.

During a exoplanet transit, starlight traverses the planetary limb. The effective opaque radius varies with wavelength because the altitude of slant optical depth near unity depends on molecular absorption and scattering. Differencing the in-transit and out-of-transit stellar spectra measures this wavelength-dependent blocked area, the exoplanet transmission spectrum. Stellar spots and faculae can contaminate that difference and require control.
During a exoplanet secondary eclipse, the disappearance of planetary light permits subtraction of the stellar contribution. Visible planetary light is predominantly reflected starlight, sensitive to clouds, hazes, Rayleigh scattering, and atomic sodium and potassium absorption. Infrared planetary emission and limb absorption show rotational-vibrational features of species such as water, carbon monoxide, carbon dioxide and methane, together with collision-induced absorption involving molecular hydrogen. Thermal emission also depends on the atmospheric temperature-pressure profile; a temperature inversion can turn a molecular absorption feature into emission. Which species are prominent depends on composition, temperature and the observed band, rather than being universal to every planet.

The measured mass and radius imply
ρˉ​p​=ρ⊕​2.636.6​≃2.1gcm−3.
(184)
Compared with the supplied composition curves, this is inconsistent with a bare iron-rich or ordinary rock-only planet. A volatile-rich interior and/or an extended low-density gas envelope is needed. A water-rich body with an atmosphere and a rocky core with a modest H/He envelope are different plausible families; mass and radius do not uniquely determine the composition.[ref]
For the requested H/He estimate, assume a hydrostatic, approximately isothermal terminator at the zero-Bond-albedo, fully redistributed equilibrium temperature. The orbit and temperature are
a=[4π2G(0.16M⊙​)P2​]1/3=0.0144AU,Teq​=30002a0.21R⊙​​​≃552K.
(185)
Surface gravity is g=Gm/Rp2​≃9.58ms−2. With molar mass M=2.2×10−3kgmol−1, the atmospheric scale height is
H=MgRu​T​≃2.18×105m≃218km.​
(186)
A spectral feature spanning N scale heights changes the blocked stellar fraction by the atmospheric annulus area:
Δδ≃R∗2​2Rp​NH​≃3.38×10−4N.​
(187)
Thus one scale height is about 338 parts per million in transit depth; a clear strong feature spanning roughly five scale heights is of order 1.7×10−3. The number of scale heights requires the actual opacity ratio; N≃ln(κline​/κcont​) is a useful isothermal estimate, not a supplied measured value. The true terminator temperature need not equal this redistribution estimate.
A nearly flat spectrum can result from a high-mean-molecular-mass atmosphere with a much smaller scale height, or from optically thick clouds/hazes that hide the deeper absorption features. These are the two qualitative possibilities; detailed precision data can discriminate them. In particular, the pre-2015 HST study favored clouds over the clear high-molecular-mass models it tested, so listing both physical mechanisms is not a claim that all such models fit those data equally well.[ref]

The circumstellar habitable zone is the range of stellar irradiation at which a suitable rocky planet could maintain liquid water at its surface under specified atmospheric conditions. It is not a guarantee of life or even of liquid water on every planet at that distance. Its boundaries depend on greenhouse gases, clouds, humidity, pressure, albedo, rotation and the stellar spectrum; stellar evolution, ultraviolet activity, atmospheric loss and tidal locking can complicate applications to cool stars.
Approximating both stars as blackbodies, the host luminosity relative to the Sun is
L⊙​L∗​​=0.212(57783000​)4≃0.00320.
(188)
The Earth-irradiance orbit therefore has
aE​=L∗​/L⊙​​AU≃0.0566AU,θmax​≃14.6pcaE​​=3.88mas.​
(189)
Use the largest projected separation and a visible reference wavelength of 550nm. The Rayleigh criterion for a circular aperture gives
D≳θmax​1.22λ​≃35.7(550nmλ​)m.​
(190)
This is only a diffraction-based minimum: detecting a faint planet beside its star additionally requires contrast suppression and adequate photon counts. An interferometer baseline, rather than its collecting-aperture diameter, sets its angular resolution.
For reflected light the reflected-light planetary phase curve gives the flux ratio ϵ=Ag​Φ(α)(R⊕​/aE​)2, where Ag​ is geometric albedo and Φ(0)=1. Numerically,
ϵfull​≃5.66×10−7Ag​.​
(191)
A unit-geometric-albedo reference gives about 6×10−7; an Earth-like chosen Ag​=0.3 gives 1.7×10−7. Albedo and phase function were not specified, so an exact contrast cannot be inferred just from the radius. Full-phase brightness occurs close to zero projected separation for an edge-on orbit; at the best-resolved quadrature, a Lambert sphere has Φ(π/2)=1/π, reducing the Earth-albedo example to 5.4×10−8. Thus the best angular separation and maximum reflected contrast are not generally achieved at the same phase.
